# Aster-9 Internal Hypoxia Reporter Assay

> Controlled demonstration document. Aster-9, Lumen-R7, and Vela-B are
> fictional names created for K-LIB evaluation. This is not a real laboratory
> or clinical protocol and must not be used for biological work.

## Culture eligibility

Use an Aster-9 reporter culture only between passages 6 and 11 inclusive and
only when confluence is between 72% and 78%. Record the passage and confluence
before adding the reporter reagent.

## Reporter priming

Add 7.5 microliters of Lumen-R7 to each 2.0 milliliters of culture medium.
Incubate for 14 minutes at 33 degrees Celsius before beginning the hypoxia
pulse.

## Hypoxia pulse

Expose the primed culture to 1.7% oxygen for 42 minutes at 33 degrees Celsius
while maintaining 5% carbon dioxide. The 42-minute timer starts only after the
chamber reaches 1.7% oxygen.

## Vela-B wash

Vela-B contains 18 mM HEPES, 135 mM sodium chloride, and 4.5 mM potassium
chloride, adjusted to pH 7.28. Perform exactly two washes using 3.0 milliliters
per wash and a contact time of 20 seconds per wash.

## Reporter readout

Excite the reporter at 405 nm and measure emission at 472 nm. A valid positive
response is a normalized 472-nm ratio of at least 1.35 at minute 11 after the
second Vela-B wash.

Abort the run if either condition occurs:

1. Chamber temperature exceeds 34.2 degrees Celsius.
2. The normalized 472-nm ratio exceeds 2.10 before minute 4.

An aborted run must not be repeated using the same culture.

## Recovery sequence

After a valid readout, recover the culture for 6 minutes in ambient oxygen,
then for 9 minutes at 5% carbon dioxide and 33 degrees Celsius. The order must
not be reversed.

## 4. Oxidative phosphorylation (inner mitochondrial membrane)

The electron transport chain passes electrons from NADH and FADH2 through a series of
complexes, pumping protons (H+) into the intermembrane space to build a proton-motive
force. ATP synthase then uses the proton gradient to make ATP (chemiosmosis). Oxygen is
the final electron acceptor, forming water. Using modern consensus values (about 2.5 ATP
per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH2), complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose yields
roughly 30 to 32 ATP. Older textbooks cite 36 to 38 ATP.

## Anaerobic conditions

Without oxygen, fermentation regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue. Lactic acid
fermentation (in muscle) produces lactate; alcoholic fermentation (in yeast) produces
ethanol and CO2. Fermentation yields only the 2 net ATP from glycolysis.

# Enzymes and Enzyme Kinetics

Enzymes are biological catalysts (mostly proteins) that speed reactions by lowering the
activation energy. They are not consumed and do not change the reaction equilibrium.

## Mechanism

The substrate binds the enzyme's active site. The induced-fit model holds that the
active site changes shape slightly to fit the substrate, forming an enzyme-substrate
complex. Enzymes are specific and are sensitive to temperature and pH, each having an
optimum. Cofactors (inorganic ions) and coenzymes (organic molecules such as vitamins)
assist catalysis.

## Michaelis-Menten kinetics

For many enzymes the initial reaction velocity relates to substrate concentration by:

v0 = (Vmax * [S]) / (Km + [S])

- Vmax is the maximum velocity, approached when the enzyme is saturated with substrate.
- Km, the Michaelis constant, equals the substrate concentration at which the reaction
 rate is half of Vmax. A low Km indicates high affinity of the enzyme for its
 substrate; a high Km indicates low affinity.

# The Cell Cycle, Mitosis, and Meiosis

## The cell cycle

The eukaryotic cell cycle is interphase followed by the mitotic (M) phase. Interphase
has three parts: G1 (growth), S (DNA synthesis/replication), and G2 (growth and
preparation). Checkpoints (notably G1/S and G2/M) ensure the cell is ready to proceed;
DNA damage or incomplete replication halts the cycle.

## Mitosis

Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells and proceeds in four
phases, in order: prophase (chromatin condenses, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes
align at the metaphase plate), anaphase (sister chromatids separate to opposite poles),
and telophase (nuclear envelopes re-form). Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, producing
two cells.

## Meiosis

Meiosis produces gametes and consists of two divisions, meiosis I and meiosis II,
following a single round of DNA replication. The result is four genetically distinct
haploid cells (n), each with half the chromosome number of the diploid (2n) parent.
